analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate prescription drug prices directly with drug manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices for expensive Medicare prescription drugs, and to set prices based on what the VA pays if talks with manufacturers failed. It also required reports and pilot tests of value-based drug payment models. It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who pay Part D premiums and out-of-pocket costs, plus federal taxpayers who fund Medicare; lower negotiated prices would reduce both.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare Part D enrollees and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary to negotiate prices with manufacturers for high-cost Part D drugs and authorizes negotiations for other covered drugs.
If negotiations fail, the bill sets prices at the lower of what the VA or major federal buyers pay, creating a fallback mechanism to control costs.
Requires public reporting on drug spending and negotiations, plus CMMI pilot testing of value-based pricing models.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would accept lower prices on high-spending Medicare drugs than current law allows.

drawbacks.text: Critics argued government negotiation could reduce manufacturer revenues and thus dampen investment in new drug development.
Defining an 'appropriate price' and the VA fallback price involves administrative judgment that could be contested or litigated.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Lower drug prices for seniors and taxpayers against possible reduced incentives for pharmaceutical innovation; the bill's fallback mechanism reduces uncertainty about outcomes but the tradeoff remains substantive rather than procedural.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in February 2017, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and received no further action before the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: S. 348 was introduced on February 9, 2017, and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance, where it remained.
No committee vote, floor vote, or other action occurred during the remainder of the 115th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pharmaceutical manufacturers, since the bill's price-negotiation and VA-fallback provisions never advanced, preserving the status quo for Medicare drug pricing.

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to Senate Finance.

for.name: Sen. Jack Reed and Sen. Sherrod Brown

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action after referral.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have negotiated lower Medicare drug prices, cutting into revenue on high-spending Part D drugs.
